analysis.one_liner: Protects college athletes' name-image-likeness earnings, health coverage, and transfer rights, while locking in a cap on school payments.
analysis.headline: The Senate voted 74-24 on September 15 and 77-22 on September 17, 2026 to open debate on the bipartisan bill; it is still pending and has not received a final vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill writes into law college athletes' right to earn money from their name, image, and likeness, and adds health coverage, scholarship, transfer, and agent protections. At the same time, it makes permanent the cap on how much athletic departments must share revenue with athletes under a court-approved settlement, and gives schools and conferences a limited exemption from antitrust law to jointly sell their TV rights. The bill passed out of the Senate Commerce Committee in June and cleared two Senate votes in September to begin debate, but has not gotten a final vote in either chamber.
analysis.who_benefits: College athletes, especially Division I players, gain enforceable rights: schools can no longer restrict their name-image-likeness earnings, scholarships can't be pulled for injury or poor performance, athletes get one transfer without losing eligibility, medical costs from sports injuries are covered during and for five years after playing, agents must register and cap fees at 5%, athletes can sue over agent misconduct, and forced arbitration clauses are void for those disputes. Athletes also get at least a third of the voting seats on athletic association governing boards.

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars institutions, conferences, and the NCAA from restricting or punishing athletes for entering name, image, and likeness agreements, and requires athletes to disclose NIL deals worth more than $600.

Athletes get one transfer between schools without losing eligibility, with additional penalty-free transfers allowed if their sport is cut, their head coach leaves, they experience sexual assault or harassment, or they pursue a graduate degree.

Division I schools must cover out-of-pocket medical costs for sports injuries, independent second opinions, catastrophic insurance above $90,000 in costs, and out-of-pocket costs for five years after an athlete's last competition; athletic associations must maintain a medical fund of at least $60 million a year.

Scholarships cannot be revoked or reduced because of injury, illness, athletic performance, or roster management decisions, and former athletes who did not finish their degree can return to complete it.

Athlete agents must register with a state, cannot charge more than 5% of an endorsement deal, and athletes can sue violating agents with a private right of action; pre-dispute arbitration clauses and class-action waivers are void for these disputes.
At least one-third of the voting seats on athletic association governing boards and rules committees must be current or recently graduated student athletes.

analysis.who_pays: Athletes give up the ability to negotiate pay above the House settlement's revenue share cap, which becomes permanent with only inflation adjustments. Athletic departments and conferences fund the medical coverage and the $60 million fund, face new reporting duties, and accept a database of NIL deal values. Broadcasters negotiate against a pooled seller if schools use the new antitrust exemption, and NIL collectives face 'valid business purpose' limits on deals.
analysis.who_pays_short: Conferences, athletic departments, and some athletes

drawbacks.text: The bill makes the settlement's revenue share cap permanent (adjusted only for inflation), so athletes' share of school athletic revenue stays capped even after the court settlement expires.

It creates a limited antitrust exemption letting schools and conferences pool and sell their sports TV rights jointly, if at least 75% of Football Bowl Subdivision schools join, shielding from antitrust challenge what would otherwise look like coordinated selling.

NIL deals must serve a 'valid business purpose' and pay amounts comparable to similar non-athletes, giving schools a tool to police deals — which targets disguised recruiting payments but could also chill legitimate endorsements.
The bill explicitly stays neutral on whether college athletes are employees, leaving the bigger labor-rights question unresolved.
Key enforcement tools — the NIL value database and the Student Athlete Ombudsman office — are run by the athletic associations themselves, the same entities the rules regulate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The athlete protections are real and enforceable — health coverage, transfer rights, scholarship security, and the right to sue agents without forced arbitration would materially change athletes' lives. But the bill's core bargain trades those protections for two concessions to schools and conferences: a permanent cap on revenue sharing with athletes and an antitrust shield for pooled media-rights sales. For star football and basketball players whose market value exceeds the cap, the bill forecloses pay growth; for everyone else, the protections likely outweigh that cost. The bill is a genuine mixed result, not a one-sided win.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate voted twice — 74-24 and then 77-22 — to begin debating the bill on September 15-17, 2026; a motion to recommit it to committee and cloture motions on an amendment and the bill itself were filed that day, and no final vote has happened.

narrative.text: Sen. Ted Cruz introduced the bill on June 2, 2026, joined by Sens. Cantwell, Schmitt, and Coons, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from the start.

The Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee ordered the bill reported favorably on June 18 and reported it with an amendment in the nature of a substitute on June 24, placing it on the Senate calendar.
On September 15, 2026, the Senate invoked cloture on the motion to proceed 74-24, with 49 of 53 Republicans, 24 of 45 Democrats, and 1 of 2 independents voting yes.
On September 17, 2026, the Senate agreed to the motion to proceed 77-22, with 49 of 53 Republicans, 27 of 45 Democrats, and 1 of 2 independents voting yes.

The same day, Sen. Thune made a motion to recommit the bill to the Commerce Committee with instructions to report back with an amendment, and cloture motions were filed on amendment SA 6776 and on the bill itself; no further votes are recorded.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet. Schools, conferences, and collectives continue operating under the current settlement rules; athletes have gained nothing yet because the bill has not become law, though its two lopsided Senate votes show unusually broad support for the framework.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — debate is ongoing

industries.industry: College athletic departments, conferences, and the NCAA
industries.note: The bill locks in the settlement's revenue share cap on what schools pay athletes — made permanent with only inflation adjustments — and shields pooled media-rights sales from antitrust law, entrenching the schools' collective bargaining position against players. In exchange, schools take on binding medical coverage obligations, scholarship protections, athlete board seats, and a $60 million annual medical fund partly paid from pooled media-rights revenue.

The bill codifies that collectives can pay athletes and bars the NCAA from restricting NIL deals, but it defines collectives as 'associated entities' and prohibits payments that circumvent the revenue share cap or lack a valid business purpose, ending the era of uncapped booster-funded deals.

A joint agreement covering 75% of Football Bowl Subdivision schools could create one enormous seller of football and basketball rights, strengthening schools' hand against networks, while the bill's market-level broadcast access provision points toward keeping games available in local markets. The bill also lets athletic associations fund their medical program with pooled media-rights revenue.

Agents gain a defined, legitimate role in college NIL deals but face mandatory state registration, a 5% fee cap on endorsement contracts, contract-form requirements, and a private right of action for athletes — rules written to protect athletes from exploitative representation.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is on the Senate floor with unusually strong support — two votes of 74-24 and 77-22 to open debate — and cloture motions pending on the bill and an amendment. If those motions succeed, the Senate could vote on amendments and final passage, though Sen. Thune's recommitted-amendment motion signals negotiation over details. With the House never having acted, final enactment before the 119th Congress ends January 3, 2027 is possible but far from certain; if the Senate stalls, the bill would die without a final vote.
